claim: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is the most aggressive human primary brain cancer.
source: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is the most aggressive human primary brain cancer.
evidence: This is a statement of established medical knowledge about GBM classification.

claim: Genetic inactivation of Atmin strongly suppresses GBM formation in Trp53-deficient mice.
source: Using a Trp53-deficient mouse model of GBM, we show that genetic inactivation of the Atm cofactor Atmin, which is dispensable for embryonic and adult neural development, strongly suppresses GBM formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the mouse model described in the manuscript.

claim: Atmin is dispensable for embryonic and adult neural development.
source: Using a Trp53-deficient mouse model of GBM, we show that genetic inactivation of the Atm cofactor Atmin, which is dispensable for embryonic and adult neural development, strongly suppresses GBM formation.
evidence: This is supported by prior published work referenced in the manuscript.

claim: Atmin deletion normalizes expression of several GBM-associated genes including Pdgfra in the Trp53-null background.
source: Mechanistically, expression of several GBM-associated genes, including Pdgfra, was normalized by Atmin deletion in the Trp53-null background.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression profiling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Pharmacological ATM inhibition reduces Pdgfra expression.
source: Pharmacological ATM inhibition also reduced Pdgfra expression, and reduced the proliferation of Trp53-deficient primary glioma cells from murine and human tumors, while normal neural stem cells were unaffected.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using ATM inhibitors on cells.

claim: Pharmacological ATM inhibition reduces proliferation of Trp53-deficient primary glioma cells from murine and human tumors.
source: Pharmacological ATM inhibition also reduced Pdgfra expression, and reduced the proliferation of Trp53-deficient primary glioma cells from murine and human tumors, while normal neural stem cells were unaffected.
evidence: This is supported by proliferation assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Normal neural stem cells are unaffected by pharmacological ATM inhibition.
source: Pharmacological ATM inhibition also reduced Pdgfra expression, and reduced the proliferation of Trp53-deficient primary glioma cells from murine and human tumors, while normal neural stem cells were unaffected.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing effects on normal versus tumor cells.

claim: PDGFRA expression is significantly increased in human TP53-mutant compared with TP53-wild-type tumors.
source: Analysis of GBM datasets showed that PDGFRA expression is also significantly increased in human TP53-mutant compared with TP53-wild-type tumors.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of TCGA database presented in the manuscript.

claim: Combined treatment with ATM and PDGFRA inhibitors efficiently kills TP53-mutant primary human GBM cells.
source: Moreover, combined treatment with ATM and PDGFRA inhibitors efficiently killed TP53-mutant primary human GBM cells, but not untransformed neural stem cells.
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Combined treatment with ATM and PDGFRA inhibitors does not kill untransformed neural stem cells.
source: Moreover, combined treatment with ATM and PDGFRA inhibitors efficiently killed TP53-mutant primary human GBM cells, but not untransformed neural stem cells.
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data comparing tumor and normal cells.

claim: ATMIN-dependent ATM signaling has a pro-tumorigenic role in TP53-deficient GBM.
source: These results reveal a new requirement for ATMIN-dependent ATM signaling in TP53-deficient GBM, indicating a pro-tumorigenic role for ATM in the context of these tumors.
evidence: This is inferred from the collective experimental results showing tumor suppression upon ATM/ATMIN loss.

claim: Standard treatment for GBM patients involves a combination of temozolomide and radiotherapy.
source: The standard treatment for GBM patients involves a combination of the DNA damaging agent temozolomide together with radiotherapy (Stupp et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published clinical practice.

claim: Current GBM treatment regimes result in severe side effects, drug resistance, and inevitable tumor recurrence.
source: However, the benefits of current treatment regimes come with severe side effects for patients, as well as drug resistance and inevitable recurrence of the tumor (Wen and Kesari, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published clinical literature.

claim: Activation of growth factor receptor signaling is a core deregulated pathway in human GBM.
source: This has identified activation of growth factor receptor signaling (for example by amplification or overexpression of the PDGF receptor) and direct or indirect inactivation of the TP53 and retinoblastoma tumor suppressors as core deregulated pathways in human GBM (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to TCGA analysis.

claim: Inactivation of TP53 and retinoblastoma tumor suppressors are core deregulated pathways in human GBM.
source: This has identified activation of growth factor receptor signaling (for example by amplification or overexpression of the PDGF receptor) and direct or indirect inactivation of the TP53 and retinoblastoma tumor suppressors as core deregulated pathways in human GBM (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to TCGA analysis.

claim: Available PDGFR inhibitors have lacked clinical impact in GBM.
source: Unfortunately, many of these pathways are difficult to target pharmacologically in vivo, and for others, like PDGFR signaling, available inhibitors have so far lacked clinical impact (Wen et al., 2006; Rich et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical trial literature.

claim: ATM is known primarily as a tumor suppressor through its role in the response to DNA double-strand breaks.
source: The DNA damage kinase ATM is known primarily as a tumor suppressor, through its role in the response to DNA double-strand breaks (Shiloh and Ziv, 2013), and systemic loss of ATM has previously been shown to accelerate glioblastoma progression (Squatrito et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on ATM function.

claim: Systemic loss of ATM accelerates glioblastoma progression.
source: The DNA damage kinase ATM is known primarily as a tumor suppressor, through its role in the response to DNA double-strand breaks (Shiloh and Ziv, 2013), and systemic loss of ATM has previously been shown to accelerate glioblastoma progression (Squatrito et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Activation of the DNA damage response in precancerous lesions acts as a barrier to tumorigenesis.
source: This tumor suppressive role is in line with the activation of the DNA damage response in precancerous lesions as a barrier to tumorigenesis (Bartkova et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Loss of ATM signaling inhibits growth of TP53-null tumor xenografts via stabilization of p14ARF.
source: A recent study has, however, demonstrated loss of ATM signaling to inhibit the growth of TP53-null tumor xenografts, via stabilization of p14ARF (Velimezi et al., 2013), suggesting that ATM function in cancer is highly context-dependent.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: ATM function in cancer is highly context-dependent.
source: A recent study has, however, demonstrated loss of ATM signaling to inhibit the growth of TP53-null tumor xenografts, via stabilization of p14ARF (Velimezi et al., 2013), suggesting that ATM function in cancer is highly context-dependent.
evidence: This is inferred from contrasting observations about ATM function in different contexts.

claim: ATM signaling occurs in response to cellular stresses other than DNA breaks.
source: As well as its canonical activation at break sites, ATM signaling also occurs in response to other cellular stresses (Bakkenist and Kastan, 2003), and this mode of ATM signaling requires the ATM INteractor ATMIN (Kanu and Behrens, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Non-canonical ATM signaling requires ATMIN.
source: As well as its canonical activation at break sites, ATM signaling also occurs in response to other cellular stresses (Bakkenist and Kastan, 2003), and this mode of ATM signaling requires the ATM INteractor ATMIN (Kanu and Behrens, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: ATMIN interacts with ATM kinase in basal conditions and dissociates from ATM in response to ionizing radiation.
source: ATMIN interacts with the ATM kinase in basal conditions and disassociates from ATM in response to ionizing radiation, to allow ATM to interact with the MRN complex at double-strand break sites (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: ATMIN has ATM-independent functions including transcriptional activation of Dynll1.
source: ATMIN also has ATM-independent functions, most notably the transcriptional activation of Dynll1, a motor protein involved with ciliogenesis and crucial for lung development (Jurado et al., 2012a; Goggolidou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: ATMIN counteracts oxidative damage in the brain.
source: In addition, ATMIN has been shown to counteract oxidative damage in the brain (Kanu et al., 2010) and to protect against B cell lymphomagenesis (Loizou et al., 2011), but its role in other cancer types has not yet been determined.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: ATMIN protects against B cell lymphomagenesis.
source: In addition, ATMIN has been shown to counteract oxidative damage in the brain (Kanu et al., 2010) and to protect against B cell lymphomagenesis (Loizou et al., 2011), but its role in other cancer types has not yet been determined.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: TP53 is a key downstream mediator of the DNA damage response pathway.
source: A key downstream mediator of the DNA damage response pathway, activated by both the double-strand break and ATMIN-dependent responses, is the tumor suppressor TP53.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DNA damage response pathways.

claim: Precancerous lesions with activated DNA damage response are under selective pressure to lose or mutate TP53.
source: Precancerous lesions in which the DNA damage response is activated are under selective pressure to lose or mutate TP53, and loss of TP53 is known to cooperate with several genes to accelerate tumorigenesis (as summarized in the IARC database [Petitjean et al., 2007]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the IARC database.

claim: Loss of ATM cooperates with Trp53 deficiency to accelerate T-cell lymphoma progression.
source: Among these cooperating changes is loss of ATM, which induces rapid T-cell lymphoma development (Westphal et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: TP53 is one of the most commonly mutated genes in human GBM.
source: TP53 is also one of the most commonly mutated genes in human GBM.
evidence: This is established knowledge from genomic studies of GBM.

claim: The majority of available mouse models of GBM use deletion of one or both copies of the Trp53 gene in combination with other mutations.
source: Consequently, the majority of available mouse models of GBM use deletion of one or both copies of the Trp53 gene in combination with other mutations (Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review of GBM models.

claim: Overexpression of Pdgfrb in adult Nestin-positive neural stem cells results in glioma formation that is accelerated in a Trp53-mutant background.
source: Overexpression of the Pdgf receptor ligand Pdgfrb in adult Nestin-positive neural stem cells, for instance, results in glioma formation, which is accelerated in a Trp53-mutant background (Squatrito et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Congenital loss of Trp53 in the mouse brain is sufficient to precipitate spontaneous glioblastoma formation.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that congenital loss of Trp53 in the mouse brain is sufficient to precipitate spontaneous glioblastoma formation, and that this correlates with upregulation of Pdgfra.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the p53ΔN mouse model.

claim: Spontaneous glioblastoma formation in p53ΔN mice correlates with upregulation of Pdgfra.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that congenital loss of Trp53 in the mouse brain is sufficient to precipitate spontaneous glioblastoma formation, and that this correlates with upregulation of Pdgfra.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression and protein data from the model.

claim: ATMIN plays a critical role in GBM formation by promoting Pdgfra protein and gene expression in a Trp53-deficient background.
source: Further, we show that ATMIN plays a critical role in GBM formation, promoting Pdgfra protein and gene expression in a Trp53-deficient background, using an in vivo glioma model as well as neural stem cell and primary tumor cell cultures.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from multiple model systems.

claim: Combining ATM inhibition with PDGFRA inhibition results in synergistic tumor cell killing with minimal effects on untransformed cells.
source: Importantly, we find that these results are translatable to therapeutic ATM inhibition in human patient-derived GBM stem cells, and that combining ATM inhibition with PDGFRA inhibition results in synergistic tumor cell killing with minimal effects on untransformed cells.
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data with combination treatment.

claim: Loss of TP53 is one of the earliest occurring events in human GBM initiation.
source: Loss of TP53 is one of the earliest occurring events in human GBM initiation (Maher et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2009; Ohgaki et al., 2004; Mazor et al., 2015; Johnson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Brain tumors arose in p53ΔN mice with high penetrance after 8 months.
source: After 8 months, brain tumors arose in p53ΔN mice with high penetrance (Figure 1A and B), similar to previous observations using an hGFAP-Cre model (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: p53ΔN mice began to show neurological symptoms at an average age of 263 days.
source: Animals began to show neurological symptoms including reduced movements and tremor at an average age of 263 days.
evidence: This is observational data from the mouse cohort.

claim: 82% of p53ΔN mice showed diffusely infiltrative astrocytic brain tumors.
source: Out of 17 animals, 14 (82%) showed diffusely infiltrative astrocytic brain tumors, the majority of which were classified as GBM by independent analysis (57% Grade IV, glioblastoma; 29% Grade III, anaplastic astrocytoma; 14% Grade II, fibrillary astrocytoma), while one displayed an osteosarcoma (Figure 1B and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis data shown in figures.

claim: 57% of p53ΔN brain tumors were classified as Grade IV glioblastoma.
source: Out of 17 animals, 14 (82%) showed diffusely infiltrative astrocytic brain tumors, the majority of which were classified as GBM by independent analysis (57% Grade IV, glioblastoma; 29% Grade III, anaplastic astrocytoma; 14% Grade II, fibrillary astrocytoma), while one displayed an osteosarcoma (Figure 1B and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by histological grading data.

claim: p53ΔN GBMs displayed pseudopalisading necrosis, microvascular proliferation with endothelial hyperplasia, and occasional endovascular thrombosis.
source: p53ΔN GBMs displayed pseudopalisading necrosis (i), microvascular proliferation with endothelial hyperplasia (ii) and occasional endovascular thrombosis (iii), hallmarks of human GBM tumors (Figure 1E [i–iii]).
evidence: This is supported by histological images in Figure 1E.

claim: p53ΔN tumors expressed Gfap, Nestin, and Olig2 markers.
source: The markers Gfap (iv), Nestin (v), and Olig2 (vi) were expressed in all tumors, while they were negative for the neuronal marker NeuN, supporting the diagnosis of glioma (Figure 1E (iv–vi) and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 1E.

claim: p53ΔN tumors were negative for the neuronal marker NeuN.
source: The markers Gfap (iv), Nestin (v), and Olig2 (vi) were expressed in all tumors, while they were negative for the neuronal marker NeuN, supporting the diagnosis of glioma (Figure 1E (iv–vi) and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Intertumoral and intratumoral heterogeneity was frequently observed in p53ΔN tumors.
source: Intertumoral and intratumoral heterogeneity, a classic hallmark of high-grade gliomas, was also frequently observed (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by histological images in Figure 1F.

claim: Early embryonic loss of Trp53 in the brain is sufficient to promote GBM formation.
source: These data indicate that early embryonic loss of Trp53 in the brain is sufficient to promote GBM formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the tumor formation data in p53ΔN mice.

claim: p53ΔN gliomas develop as a result of secondary mutations arising in the Trp53-null brain.
source: The long latency of these tumors, together with the genome instability and transcriptional changes known to be induced by loss of Trp53, indicated that these gliomas almost certainly develop as a result of secondary mutations arising in the Trp53-null brain.
evidence: This is inferred from the long latency and known effects of Trp53 loss.

claim: Mouse SNP array data revealed large chromosomal gains and losses in four out of five analyzed p53ΔN gliomas.
source: In line with this notion, mouse SNP array data revealed large chromosomal gains and losses (typical tumorigenic genetic changes) in four out of five analyzed p53ΔNgliomas, whereas no changes were detected in one wt and three Trp53-deficient non-tumorigenic control NS cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by SNP array data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: No chromosomal changes were detected in wild-type and Trp53-deficient non-tumorigenic control neural stem cells.
source: In line with this notion, mouse SNP array data revealed large chromosomal gains and losses (typical tumorigenic genetic changes) in four out of five analyzed p53ΔNgliomas, whereas no changes were detected in one wt and three Trp53-deficient non-tumorigenic control NS cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by SNP array data.

claim: AtminΔN; p53ΔN mice showed significantly longer tumor-free survival than p53ΔN animals (p<0.0002).
source: Strikingly, AtminΔN; p53ΔN mice showed significantly longer tumor-free survival than p53ΔNanimals (p<0.0002) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival data in Figure 2A.

claim: 43% of AtminΔN; p53ΔN mice did not develop any signs of sickness and were still alive after 450 days.
source: The largest proportion of AtminΔN; p53ΔNmice (43%) did not develop any signs of sickness and were still alive after 450 days; a further 36% succumbed either to non-tumor-related illness or, in one case, a pancreatic tumor (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by cohort status data in Figure 2B.

claim: Only 21% of AtminΔN; p53ΔN double mutants initiated glial tumors compared with 82% of p53ΔN mice.
source: Only three animals out of a cohort of 14 AtminΔN; p53ΔNdouble mutants (21%) initiated glial tumors (Figure 2B), compared with 82% of p53ΔNmice over the same period.
evidence: This is supported by tumor incidence data in Figure 2B.

claim: The three GBMs arising in AtminΔN; p53ΔN double-mutant mice did not escape Atmin deletion.
source: The three GBMs arising in AtminΔN; p53ΔNdouble-mutant mice arose later but were histologically similar to those observed in p53ΔN mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and did not escape Atmin deletion, suggesting that the requirement for Atmin can eventually be overcome, but only in a small proportion of cases.
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis of the tumors.

claim: Central nervous system deletion of Atmin alone did not affect brain morphology or histology.
source: Importantly, central nervous system deletion of Atmin alone (AtminΔN) did not affect brain morphology or histology (Kanu et al., 2010) and the mice remained tumor free (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and survival data in Figure 2A.

claim: Atmin deletion rescues the increased proliferation of p53ΔN NSCs.
source: p53ΔNNSCs proliferated more rapidly than wild-type (wt) controls. This proliferative advantage, however, was rescued in AtminΔN; p53ΔN NSCs (Figure 2C and D), indicating that Atmin is required for the hyperproliferation of Trp53-deficient NSCs.
evidence: This is supported by proliferation assay data in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Loss of Atmin alone did not alter proliferation of NSCs.
source: Loss of Atmin alone did not alter proliferation of NSCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by proliferation data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: p53ΔN NSCs arrested less efficiently than wt NSCs in response to ionizing radiation.
source: As expected, p53ΔN NSCs arrested less efficiently than wt NSCs and cell death was reduced; but cell cycle arrest and cell death were not rescued in AtminΔN; p53ΔN NSCs (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle arrest data in figures.

claim: Cell cycle arrest and cell death in response to IR were not rescued in AtminΔN; p53ΔN NSCs.
source: As expected, p53ΔN NSCs arrested less efficiently than wt NSCs and cell death was reduced; but cell cycle arrest and cell death were not rescued in AtminΔN; p53ΔN NSCs (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in figures.

claim: p53ΔN NSCs were more resilient to hypoxia-induced death than wild-type NSCs.
source: In addition to IR-induced cell death, p53ΔN NSCs were more resilient to hypoxia-induced death, consistent with previous studies (Liu et al., 2007; Graeber et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to prior work.

claim: Atmin deletion re-sensitized p53ΔN NSCs to hypoxia to similar levels as wt NSCs.
source: Atmin deletion in these cells re-sensitized them to hypoxia, to similar levels as wt NSCs (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by hypoxia-induced cell death data in Figure 2F.

claim: Five out of five animals injected with p53ΔN NSCs died within 93 days post-injection.
source: Five out of five animals injected with p53ΔN NSCs died within 93 days post-injection, while four out of five wt and three out of four p53ΔN; AtminΔNNSC-injected animals were still alive even at 155 days, the endpoint of the experiment (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by survival data from orthotopic transplant experiments in Figure 2G.

claim: Four out of five wt NSC-injected animals were still alive at 155 days post-injection.
source: Five out of five animals injected with p53ΔN NSCs died within 93 days post-injection, while four out of five wt and three out of four p53ΔN; AtminΔNNSC-injected animals were still alive even at 155 days, the endpoint of the experiment (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by survival data in Figure 2G.

claim: Three out of four AtminΔN; p53ΔN NSC-injected animals were still alive at 155 days post-injection.
source: Five out of five animals injected with p53ΔN NSCs died within 93 days post-injection, while four out of five wt and three out of four p53ΔN; AtminΔNNSC-injected animals were still alive even at 155 days, the endpoint of the experiment (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by survival data in Figure 2G.

claim: Genetic inactivation of Atmin greatly impairs the tumorigenic potential of p53ΔN cells.
source: Thus, genetic inactivation of Atmin greatly impairs the tumorigenic potential of p53ΔNcells.
evidence: This is inferred from the orthotopic transplant survival data.

claim: 145 genes were downregulated more than 1.5-fold in p53ΔN NSCs compared with wt NSCs.
source: Compared with wt NSCs, 145 genes were downregulated more than 1.5-fold in p53ΔN, whereas 77 were overexpressed (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 77 genes were overexpressed more than 1.5-fold in p53ΔN NSCs compared with wt NSCs.
source: Compared with wt NSCs, 145 genes were downregulated more than 1.5-fold in p53ΔN, whereas 77 were overexpressed (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data in Figure 3A.

claim: Canonical Trp53 target genes such as Bax, Puma, and Cdkn1a were downregulated to a similar extent in AtminΔN; p53ΔN compared with p53ΔN NSCs.
source: Many of the canonical Trp53 target genes, such as Bax, Puma, and Cdkn1a, were downregulated to a similar extent in AtminΔN; p53ΔN compared with p53ΔNNSCs.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data from microarray analysis.

claim: 27% of genes deregulated in p53ΔN NSCs returned to wt expression levels when Atmin was also deleted.
source: However, 27% of genes deregulated in p53ΔNNSCs returned to wt expression levels when Atmin was also deleted (36/145 of the decreased, and 24/77 of the increased genes; examples in Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis.

claim: Abnormal levels of genes rescued in double mutant NSCs were found to be associated with human GBM in TCGA database.
source: When this subset of genes 'rescued' in double mutant NSCs was queried against the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database, in several cases abnormal levels of these transcripts were found to be associated with human GBM (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2008; Suvasini et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of TCGA data.

claim: Elevated levels of PDGFRA have been observed in human gliomas of various malignancy grades.
source: Elevated levels of PDGFRA have been observed in human gliomas of various malignancy grades (Engström et al., 2012), and increased PDGFR signaling has been shown to induce glioma-like growths in vivo (Jackson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Increased PDGFR signaling induces glioma-like growths in vivo.
source: Elevated levels of PDGFRA have been observed in human gliomas of various malignancy grades (Engström et al., 2012), and increased PDGFR signaling has been shown to induce glioma-like growths in vivo (Jackson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Increased PDGFRA levels are a characteristic hallmark of the proneural GBM subtype.
source: Increased PDGFRA levels are also a characteristic hallmark of the proneural GBM subtype as classified in (Brennan et al., 2013; Verhaak et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to GBM classification studies.

claim: p53ΔN NSCs were associated most closely with the proneural GBM subtype.
source: Interestingly, we found that p53ΔNNSCs were associated most closely with the proneural subtype when comparing the microarray expression profile from the murine NSCs to that of publically available human GBM samples from TCGA (Verhaak et al., 2010) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), which is in agreement with elevated Pdgfra mRNA as well as protein levels (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of expression profiles shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: p53ΔN NSCs have elevated Pdgfra mRNA and protein levels.
source: Interestingly, we found that p53ΔNNSCs were associated most closely with the proneural subtype when comparing the microarray expression profile from the murine NSCs to that of publically available human GBM samples from TCGA (Verhaak et al., 2010) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), which is in agreement with elevated Pdgfra mRNA as well as protein levels (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and Western blot data in Figure 3D.

claim: Increased Pdgfra protein expression was apparent in high-grade GBMs from endstage p53ΔN animals.
source: This increased protein expression was also apparent in high-grade GBMs from endstage p53ΔNanimals (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 3E.

claim: Other growth factor receptors like Egfr and proteins commonly deregulated in glioma remained unaltered in p53ΔN cells and tumors.
source: Other growth factor receptors, like Egfr, and proteins commonly deregulated in glioma including Rb, Pten, Cyclin D2, Junc, and Cdk4 (Wang et al., 2009) remained unaltered in p53ΔNcells and tumors (Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3), as did the closely related Pdgf receptor Pdgfrb and the receptor ligands Pdgfa and Pdgfb (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and expression data in supplementary figures.

claim: Deletion of Atmin together with Trp53 completely rescued the elevated Pdgfra expression, reducing it to wild-type levels.
source: Importantly, deletion of Atmin together with Trp53 completely rescued the elevated Pdgfra expression, reducing it to wild-type levels (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and Western blot data in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Overexpression of tagged Atmin in double mutant NSCs restored elevated Pdgfra expression at both the mRNA and protein levels.
source: Overexpression of tagged Atmin in double mutant NSCs restored elevated Pdgfra expression at both the mRNA and protein levels (Figure 3F and G), while acute silencing of Atmin in p53ΔNNSCs, using two independent shRNA constructs, reduced Pdgfra levels (Figure 3H), implying that sustained Pdgfra upregulation in p53ΔNNSCs constantly requires Atmin function to maintain increased Pdgfra expression.
evidence: This is supported by overexpression experiment data in Figure 3F and G.

claim: Acute silencing of Atmin in p53ΔN NSCs reduced Pdgfra levels.
source: Overexpression of tagged Atmin in double mutant NSCs restored elevated Pdgfra expression at both the mRNA and protein levels (Figure 3F and G), while acute silencing of Atmin in p53ΔNNSCs, using two independent shRNA constructs, reduced Pdgfra levels (Figure 3H), implying that sustained Pdgfra upregulation in p53ΔNNSCs constantly requires Atmin function to maintain increased Pdgfra expression.
evidence: This is supported by shRNA knockdown data in Figure 3H.

claim: Stable knockdown of Pdgfra resulted in a significant decrease in the proliferation rate of primary p53ΔN tumor cells.
source: To assess whether Trp53 null tumors require sustained Pdgfra overexpression, we isolated primary tumor cells from GBM-bearing p53ΔNmice and induced stable knockdown of Pdgfra using shRNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 5). This resulted in a significant decrease in the proliferation rate of these primary tumor cells (Figure 3I), emphasizing the importance of Atmin function in supporting elevated Pdgfra expression in p53ΔNgliomas.
evidence: This is supported by proliferation assay data in Figure 3I.

claim: Treatment with an Atm inhibitor significantly reduced Pdgfra transcript and protein levels in p53ΔN primary tumor cells.
source: Treatment with an Atm inhibitor (ATMi) significantly reduced Pdgfra transcript and protein levels (Figure 4A and B) and efficiently reduced proliferation of p53∆Nprimary tumor cells (Figure 4C), similar to our observations after Pdgfra silencing.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and Western blot data in Figure 4A and B.

claim: ATM inhibitor treatment efficiently reduced proliferation of p53ΔN primary tumor cells.
source: Treatment with an Atm inhibitor (ATMi) significantly reduced Pdgfra transcript and protein levels (Figure 4A and B) and efficiently reduced proliferation of p53∆Nprimary tumor cells (Figure 4C), similar to our observations after Pdgfra silencing.
evidence: This is supported by proliferation data in Figure 4C.

claim: ATMi treatment reduced Pdgfra expression in p53ΔN NSCs.
source: ATMi treatment also reduced Pdgfra expression in p53ΔNNSCs (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data in Figure 4D.

claim: Atm-/-; p53ΔN double-mutant NSCs had dramatically lower Pdgfra expression levels than p53ΔN NSCs, comparable to AtminΔN; p53ΔN and wt NSCs.
source: Consistent with these results, Atm-/-; p53ΔNdouble-mutant NSCs had dramatically lower Pdgfra expression levels than p53ΔNNSCs, comparable to AtminΔN; p53ΔNand wt NSCs (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and Western blot data in Figure 4E and F.

claim: Genetic loss of Atm reduced the proliferation of p53ΔN NSCs to wt levels.
source: Furthermore, in vitro proliferation assays showed that genetic loss of Atm reduced the proliferation of p53ΔNNSCs to wt levels (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by proliferation assay data in Figure 4G.

claim: Mice injected with Atm-/-; p53ΔN NSCs survived up to 50% longer than those receiving p53ΔN NSCs.
source: Importantly, the reduction in cell proliferation in vitro correlated with reduced tumorigenic potential of the NSCs when orthotopically injected into the brains of NOD/SCID mice. Mice injected with Atm-/-; p53ΔNNSCs survived up to 50% longer than those receiving p53ΔNNSCs (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by survival data from orthotopic transplants in Figure 4H.

claim: Atmin deletion was more effective than deletion of Atm in suppressing tumorigenicity.
source: However, Atmin deletion (Figure 2G) was more effective than deletion of Atm (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing survival data in Figure 2G and Figure 4H.

claim: Neither p53ΔN nor AtminΔN; p53ΔN NSCs showed increased γh2ax or 53bp1 foci in basal conditions.
source: Neither p53ΔNnor AtminΔN; p53ΔNNSCs showed increased γh2ax or 53bp1 foci in basal conditions (Figure 5A and B), suggesting that the different proliferation rates are not caused by changes in endogenous DNA damage.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Pdgfra expression was not affected by IR or hydroxyurea in wt or p53ΔN NSCs.
source: Pdgfra expression was not affected by IR or hydroxyurea (HU), two well-described inducers of ATM signaling, either in wt or in p53ΔNNSCs (Figure 5C) and no increased Atm substrate phosphorylation could be detected in untreated p53ΔN NSCs (Figure 5D), suggesting that Pdgfra upregulation is not a consequence of stimulation of DNA damage signaling.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data in Figure 5C.

claim: No increased Atm substrate phosphorylation could be detected in untreated p53ΔN NSCs.
source: Pdgfra expression was not affected by IR or hydroxyurea (HU), two well-described inducers of ATM signaling, either in wt or in p53ΔNNSCs (Figure 5C) and no increased Atm substrate phosphorylation could be detected in untreated p53ΔN NSCs (Figure 5D), suggesting that Pdgfra upregulation is not a consequence of stimulation of DNA damage signaling.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 5D.

claim: Atm substrate phosphorylation was comparable in IR- and HU-treated wt, p53ΔN and AtminΔN; p53ΔN NSCs.
source: Atm substrate phosphorylation was also comparable in IR- and HU-treated wt, p53ΔNand AtminΔN; p53ΔNNSCs (Figure 5D), suggesting that the response to DNA damage stimuli is comparable in these cells.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 5D.

claim: PDGFRA expression was significantly increased in two out of three human GNSC lines compared with untransformed human neural stem cells.
source: PDGFRA expression was significantly increased in two out of three human GNSC lines compared with untransformed human neural stem cells (cb660; (Engström et al., 2012; Pollard et al., 2009) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 6B.

claim: Higher average PDGFRA expression was observed in TP53-mutant glioblastoma samples compared with TP53 wild-type samples in both RNA-seq and microarray data.
source: The RNA-seq and microarray data were handled separately; for each, we observed higher average PDGFRA expression in TP53-mutant glioblastoma samples compared with TP53 wild-type samples (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Higher PDGFRA expression levels were observed in the Proneural and GCiMP GBM subtypes compared to Classical, Neural, and Mesenchymal subtypes.
source: We also observed higher PDGFRA expression levels in the Proneural and GCiMP GBM subtypes when compared to the Classical, Neural, and Mesenchymal (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by TCGA data analysis in Figure 6E.

claim: Treatment with an ATMi strongly reduced PDGFRA expression in GNSCs.
source: In line with the data from our mouse model, treatment with an ATMi strongly reduced PDGFRA expression in GNSCs, whereas no significant effect on PDGFRA expression was detected in cb660 controls (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data in Figure 6F.

claim: No significant effect of ATMi on PDGFRA expression was detected in cb660 control cells.
source: In line with the data from our mouse model, treatment with an ATMi strongly reduced PDGFRA expression in GNSCs, whereas no significant effect on PDGFRA expression was detected in cb660 controls (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data in Figure 6F.

claim: Depletion of PDGFRA led to a significant decrease in the proliferation rate of human GNSCs.
source: To determine whether a reduction in PDGFRA levels would be sufficient to inhibit the proliferation of primary GNSCs from human tumors, G179 cells were infected with doxycycline (dox)-inducible shRNA constructs targeting PDGFRA (Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 5), and their proliferation was monitored over a period of 10 days. In agreement with our results in the mouse, depletion of PDGFRA led to a significant decrease in the proliferation rate of human GNSCs (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is supported by proliferation data in Figure 6H.

claim: ATMi treatment reduced the proliferation rate of human TP53 mutant GNSCs, but not cb660 control cells.
source: To analyze the physiological effects of ATM inhibition on GNSCs, proliferation was monitored over a period of 7 days. Similar to our observations in murine NSCs, ATMi treatment reduced the proliferation rate of human TP53 mutant GNSCs, but not cb660 control cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by proliferation data in Figure 7A.

claim: Co-treatment of GNSCs with ATM and PDGFR inhibitors further reduced cell proliferation compared to single treatments.
source: We reasoned that ATMi-mediated reduction in PDGFRA protein levels could potentiate the effects of PDGFR inhibition. Consistent with this, we observed that co-treatment of GNSCs, but not untransformed NSCs (e.g. cb660), with relevant ATM and PDGFR inhibitor concentrations further reduced cell proliferation (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by proliferation data in Figure 7A.

claim: Combination treatment with ATM and PDGFR inhibitors induced substantial cell death in GNSCs while untransformed NSCs remained largely unaffected.
source: More detailed analysis revealed that this treatment combination induced substantial cell death, while untransformed NSCs remained largely unaffected (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is supported by cell death data in Figure 7B and C.

claim: PDGFRi treatment by itself had little effect on cell death and proliferation of GNSCs.
source: In contrast, PDGFRi treatment by itself had little effect on cell death and proliferation (Figure 7 A–C).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7A-C.

claim: ATM is required for PDGFRA overexpression in both murine and human GBM cells.
source: Hence, ATM is required for PDGFRA overexpression in both murine and human GBM cells, and combined inhibition of ATM and PDGFR induces lethality in TP53-mutant glioma cells, promising new opportunities for future GBM treatment.
evidence: This is inferred from the collective experimental results across mouse and human systems.

claim: Combined inhibition of ATM and PDGFR induces lethality in TP53-mutant glioma cells.
source: Hence, ATM is required for PDGFRA overexpression in both murine and human GBM cells, and combined inhibition of ATM and PDGFR induces lethality in TP53-mutant glioma cells, promising new opportunities for future GBM treatment.
evidence: This is supported by cell death data from combination treatment experiments.
